# Behavioral Question Pool

[← Bloomberg](../README.md) · [Every Bloomberg question](../../bloomberg.md) · [Read it on TrueInterview](https://trueinterview.io/study/behavioral-question-pool)

`deep-dive` `star` `why-company`

---

## Requirements

Create a portable bank of behavioral stories aligned with Bloomberg's recurring competency questions. Reuse the same stories across recruiter, technical resume-introduction, HR, and EM interviews, adjusting the framing slightly.

## Examples

Frequently reported prompts from recent interview loops include:

**Motivation / fit:**

- "What makes you want to join Bloomberg?" (asked at least once in every round)
- "Why this location, and why this team?"
- "What do you understand about the products we build?"
- "Why pursue an entry-level position after already gaining work experience?" (only for re-applicants)

**Project deep-dive (technical and HM rounds):**

- "Which project has been the hardest for you?"
- "What project that you delivered are you most proud of?"
- "What led to this project in the first place?"
- "What would happen to the project if you were suddenly gone?"

**Collaboration / conflict:**

- "Describe a team situation in which you ran into difficulties."
- "Tell me about a conflict you helped resolve."
- "What did you do when you received unfavorable feedback?"
- "Describe a time you had to refuse a stakeholder's request."

**Initiative / scope:**

- "Tell me about a time you showed initiative or exceeded expectations."
- "When did you accomplish more than your assigned responsibility?"
- "Describe a time you questioned something you had been asked to do."

**Self-reflection:**

- "What would your coworkers identify as your strongest quality?"
- "What is one personal area you are working to improve?"
- "Tell me about a mistake you made."

## Notes

- Five adaptable stories — one for each category — address most questions: a collaboration success, an initiative or automation example, clarifying scope amid uncertainty, recovering from a mistake, and delivering a proud impact.
- Interviewers explicitly assess the STAR format: Situation (15 seconds), Task (10 seconds), Action (60–90 seconds, naming one technical choice), and Result (15–30 seconds, using a figure where feasible).
- Bloomberg recruiters identify stock responses ("I'm a perfectionist," "I work too hard") as warning signs in candidate evaluations. Support each assertion with a specific example lasting 20–30 seconds.
- A single story can be reframed for different rounds: "delivered on a compressed schedule by reducing scope" can demonstrate collaboration, initiative, or scope clarification, based on the aspect you highlight.
- The HM interview contains the toughest behavioral deep dive. Choose one project you can explain from every angle — how it started, its trade-offs, the handoff, and what you would revise. Do not choose work in which you were merely observing.
- Recent technical interview introductions are increasingly adding a brief AI / LLM conversation — how LLM tools fit into your workflow and your view of AI in engineering — alongside the resume and BQ discussion. Prepare a concise answer with a clear point of view.
- For Data Management / DMP-track positions, the opening interview is a team-lead discussion covering your resume and behavioral topics, and resolving a disagreement with an engineering counterpart comes up regularly.

## Preparation

- Write five stories, giving each a paragraph for Situation / Task, one paragraph for Action, and one Result line. Rehearse each aloud with a timer; keep every story under 2.5 minutes.
- For every story, identify two ways to connect it to other prompts (the conflict example can also show initiative; the initiative example can also show learning from failure).
- Prepare a single-page "why Bloomberg" explanation built around three specific anchors: real-time data at scale, internally developed C++/Java distributed systems, and new-graduate training. Make one of those three personal.
- Rehearse the ending: have two questions ready about onboarding, mentoring, or the office's advancement path. Asking them is viewed as a modest positive signal in every round.
